entries.title: Object reference not set to an instance of an object
entries.explain: The code used a member (a property, a method, an index) on a variable that holds `null` instead of an object. There is nothing there to call the member on, so .NET stops the program.
causes: A variable or field was declared but never given an object (`List<int> items;` with no `= new()`).
A method returned `null` because it found nothing: `FirstOrDefault`, `Find`, a dictionary `TryGetValue`, `Console.ReadLine()` at the end of input.
A property of an object you created was never set, so reading `order.Customer.Name` fails at `Customer`.
Nullable warnings (CS8602, CS8600) were ignored: they point at exactly these lines before you run.
fix: Find which part of the line is `null`: on `a.B.C()` it can be `a` or `a.B`.
Create the object before using it (`var items = new List<int>();`).
When `null` is a real possibility, check for it: `if (person is null) return;`, or use `?.` and `??`: `person?.Name ?? "unknown"`.
entries.specific: Something used{onLine} is `null` at the moment the line runs.

entries.title: Sequence contains no elements
entries.explain: `First()`, `Last()`, `Single()`, and `Max()`, `Min()` or `Average()` over numbers all need at least one item to return. The sequence was empty (or nothing matched the condition), so there was no value to give back.
causes: The list or query really is empty, for example because a `Where` filtered everything out.
`First(x => ...)` was given a condition that no item meets.
`Max()`, `Min()` or `Average()` was called on an empty list of `int`, `double` or `decimal`.
fix: Use `FirstOrDefault()` / `LastOrDefault()` / `SingleOrDefault()` and handle the default (`null`, or `0` for numbers).
Check first: `if (items.Count == 0) ...` or `items.Any()`.
For numbers, give a fallback: `items.DefaultIfEmpty(0).Max()`.
entries.before:
var scores = new List<int>();
var best = scores.Max();   // throws: empty
entries.after:
var scores = new List<int>();
var best = scores.Count > 0 ? scores.Max() : 0;

hunt.note: Line {line} calls `{match}`, which throws when there is nothing to return.

entries.specific: The sequence used{onLine} was empty when it was asked for an element.

entries.title: Sequence contains more than one element
entries.explain: `Single()` and `SingleOrDefault()` promise that there is at most one item, and check that promise. More than one item matched, so they refuse to pick one for you.
causes: The data has duplicates you did not expect (two customers with the same email).
The condition passed to `Single(x => ...)` is looser than intended.
`SingleOrDefault` was used where `FirstOrDefault` was meant: `OrDefault` only covers zero items, not many.
fix: If any match will do, use `First()` or `FirstOrDefault()`.
If there really should be only one, tighten the condition or fix the duplicate data.
entries.before:
var names = new[] { "Ann", "Bo", "Ann" };
var ann = names.Single(n => n == "Ann");   // two matches
entries.after:
var names = new[] { "Ann", "Bo", "Ann" };
var ann = names.First(n => n == "Ann");

hunt.note: Line {line} calls `{match}`, which throws when more than one item matches.

entries.specific: More than one item matched the `Single` call{onLine}.

entries.title: Collection was modified during a foreach
entries.explain: A `foreach` loop walks a collection with an enumerator that checks the collection has not changed since the loop started. Adding to or removing from the same list or dictionary inside the loop breaks that, so the next step of the loop throws.
causes: Calling `list.Remove(x)` or `list.Add(x)` inside `foreach (var x in list)`.
Changing a dictionary's keys inside `foreach` over that dictionary.
A method called from the loop body changes the collection behind your back.
fix: To remove items, use `list.RemoveAll(x => condition)` instead of a loop.
Or loop over a copy: `foreach (var x in list.ToList())`.
Or collect changes in a second list and apply them after the loop.
entries.before:
foreach (var n in numbers)
    if (n < 0) numbers.Remove(n);   // throws on the next step
entries.after: numbers.RemoveAll(n => n < 0);

hunt.note: Line {line} changes a collection with `{match}`; if that runs inside a `foreach` over the same collection, it is the cause.

entries.specific: A collection was changed while a `foreach` was looping over it{onLine}.

entries.message: Nullable object must have a value
entries.title: Nullable object must have a value
entries.explain: A nullable value type (`int?`, `DateTime?`, `bool?`) was read with `.Value` or cast to its plain type while it held `null`. A plain `int` cannot be `null`, so there was nothing to convert.
causes: Reading `.Value` without checking `.HasValue` first.
A cast such as `(int)maybeNumber` when `maybeNumber` is `null`.
A database column or parsed field that was empty.
fix: Check before reading: `if (age.HasValue) ...` or `if (age is int a) ...`.
Supply a default: `age ?? 0` or `age.GetValueOrDefault()`.
entries.before:
int? discount = null;
int price = 100 - discount.Value;   // throws
entries.after:
int? discount = null;
int price = 100 - (discount ?? 0);

hunt.note: Line {line} reads `{match}`, which throws when it is `null`.

entries.specific: A nullable value was `null` when its value was read{onLine}.

entries.message: instance of entity type '(?<entity>[^']+)' cannot be tracked because another instance with the (?:same )?key value
entries.title: Entity cannot be tracked: another instance with the same key is tracked
entries.explain: An EF Core `DbContext` keeps exactly one object per primary key in its change tracker. The code asked it to track a second, separate object with a key it already holds, and EF Core cannot know which of the two is the truth.
causes: Loading an entity, then calling `Update` or `Attach` on a new object (often built from a request) with the same `Id`.
Adding two new objects with the same explicit key.
A long-lived context that still remembers an entity from an earlier operation.
fix: Change the entity you already loaded instead of attaching a new one: `var p = db.Products.Find(id); p.Name = name;`.
If you only read it, load it with `AsNoTracking()` so it is not tracked in the first place.
Use a short-lived context per operation.
entries.before:
var existing = db.Products.Find(1);
db.Products.Update(new Product { Id = 1, Name = "Pen" });   // throws
entries.specific: Two different `{entity}` objects with the same key reached the same context{onLine}.

entries.message: A second operation was started on this context
entries.title: A second operation was started on this context
entries.explain: A `DbContext` can run only one database operation at a time and is not thread-safe. A new query or save started while the previous one was still running on the same context.
causes: Calling an async EF Core method without `await`, then starting another query.
Running queries in parallel (`Task.WhenAll`, `Parallel.ForEach`) against one context.
Starting a query while still iterating the results of another one on the same context.
fix: `await` every EF Core async call before starting the next one.
Give each parallel task its own context (for example via `IDbContextFactory`).
Materialize the first query with `ToListAsync()` before running the next.
entries.before:
var a = db.Orders.ToListAsync();     // not awaited
var b = await db.Customers.ToListAsync();
entries.after:
var a = await db.Orders.ToListAsync();
var b = await db.Customers.ToListAsync();

hunt.note: Line {line} starts `{match}` without `await`, so it may still be running when the next query starts.

entries.specific: Two operations overlapped on one `DbContext`{onLine}.

entries.title: Operation is not valid in the current state
entries.explain: `InvalidOperationException` means the arguments were fine, but the object was not in a state where this call makes sense, for example reading from an enumerator that has finished or calling a method before setup is done. The message says which rule was broken.
causes: Calling a method in the wrong order (using something before it is started, opened or configured).
Asking for a value that does not exist right now, such as `Peek()` or `Dequeue()` on an empty `Queue` or `Stack`.
A library rule, described in the message text, was not followed.
fix: Read the message: it names the state that was wrong.
Check the state before the call (`if (queue.Count > 0)`), or use the `Try...` version (`TryDequeue`, `TryPeek`).
entries.before:
var queue = new Queue<string>();
var next = queue.Dequeue();   // Queue empty.
entries.specific: The message says: {detail}.

entries.title: The given key was not present in the dictionary
entries.explain: Reading `dict[key]` requires the key to be there; unlike some languages, C# does not hand back a default value. The key you asked for is not in the dictionary, so the indexer throws.
causes: The key was never added, or was added with different spelling or casing (`"Total"` vs `"total"`).
Extra spaces from input or parsing (`"apple "`).
Reading before the code that fills the dictionary ran.
fix: Use `TryGetValue`: `if (dict.TryGetValue(key, out var value)) ...`.
Or `dict.GetValueOrDefault(key)` when a default is fine.
For case-insensitive keys, create it with `new Dictionary<string, int>(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase)`.
entries.before:
var stock = new Dictionary<string, int> { ["apple"] = 3 };
Console.WriteLine(stock["pear"]);   // throws
entries.after:
var stock = new Dictionary<string, int> { ["apple"] = 3 };
Console.WriteLine(stock.GetValueOrDefault("pear"));
entries.specific: The dictionary has no key `{key}`{onLine}.

entries.title: Input string was not in a correct format
entries.explain: A parse or convert method (`int.Parse`, `double.Parse`, `Convert.ToInt32`, `DateTime.Parse`) was given text that is not a valid number or date in the expected format, so it cannot produce a value.
causes: The text has letters, spaces or symbols: `"12a"`, `" 7 "` is fine but `"7 kg"` is not.
An empty string `""` (for example an empty input line).
A decimal number given to `int.Parse` (`"3.5"`), or a decimal separator that differs from the current culture.
fix: Use `TryParse` and handle failure: `if (int.TryParse(text, out var n)) ...`.
Clean the text first (`text.Trim()`), and pick the right type (`double.Parse` for `"3.5"`).
For fixed formats, pass `CultureInfo.InvariantCulture`.
entries.before:
var text = "12a";
int qty = int.Parse(text);   // throws

hunt.note: Line {line} calls `{match}`, which throws when the text is not in the right format.

entries.specific: The text `{input}` could not be read as a value of the type asked for{onLine}.

entries.title: Index was outside the bounds of the array
entries.explain: Arrays (and strings) are indexed from `0` to `Length - 1`. The code used an index below 0 or at least `Length`, which points past the end, so .NET refuses to read or write there.
causes: A loop that runs one step too far: `i <= arr.Length` instead of `i < arr.Length`.
Reading `arr[arr.Length]` to get the last item (it is `arr[arr.Length - 1]`, or `arr[^1]`).
An empty array, where even `arr[0]` is out of range.
fix: Loop with `i < arr.Length`, or use `foreach` when you do not need the index.
Use `arr[^1]` for the last item, after checking `arr.Length > 0`.

hunt.note: Line {line} uses `{match}`; the last valid index is one less than the length.

entries.specific: An index used{onLine} is outside the array.

entries.title: Argument out of range
entries.explain: A method was given a number outside the range it accepts. For a `List<T>` or `string` this is usually an index or length past the end; `List<T>` reports this exception where an array would throw `IndexOutOfRangeException`.
causes: `list[i]` or `list.RemoveAt(i)` with `i` equal to or greater than `list.Count`, or negative.
`text.Substring(start, length)` where `start + length` goes past the end of the string.
A negative or too-large value for a count, capacity, month or day.
fix: Keep indexes in `0 .. Count - 1`; check `i < list.Count` before using it.
For substrings, clamp the length: `text[..Math.Min(5, text.Length)]`.
The parameter name in the message tells you which argument was wrong.
entries.before:
var word = "cat";
var start = word.Substring(0, 5);   // only 3 characters
entries.after:
var word = "cat";
var start = word[..Math.Min(5, word.Length)];
entries.specific: The argument `{param}` was out of range{onLine}.

entries.title: Value cannot be null
entries.explain: A method was handed `null` for an argument that must be a real object, and it checked this up front instead of failing later. The parameter name in the message tells you which argument was `null`.
causes: Running LINQ on a `null` collection: the parameter is then called `source`.
`int.Parse(null)` or `File.ReadAllText(null)`, often from `Console.ReadLine()` returning `null` at end of input.
A field or property that was never set, passed along to another method.
fix: Find where the value comes from and make sure it is set (`= new List<int>()`).
Handle the `null` before the call: `var line = Console.ReadLine() ?? "";`.
Do not ignore CS8604 warnings: they flag these calls at compile time.
entries.before:
List<int>? scores = null;
var total = scores.Sum();   // source is null
entries.after:
List<int> scores = new();
var total = scores.Sum();
entries.specific: The argument `{param}` was `null`{onLine}.

entries.message: same key has already been added(?:\. Key: (?<key>.+))?
entries.title: An item with the same key has already been added
entries.explain: A dictionary holds each key at most once. `Add` (and collection initializers, and `ToDictionary`) refuse to overwrite: the key was already there, so the call throws instead of silently replacing the value.
causes: Calling `dict.Add(key, value)` twice with the same key, for example in a loop over data with duplicates.
`ToDictionary(x => x.Name)` where two items share a name.
A case-insensitive dictionary where `"Ann"` and `"ann"` count as the same key.
fix: Use the indexer to add or replace: `dict[key] = value;`.
Use `TryAdd` to keep the first value and skip duplicates.
To count repeats, update the existing value: `dict[key] = dict.GetValueOrDefault(key) + 1;`.

hunt.note: Line {line} calls `{match}`, which throws when a key is already present.

entries.specific: The key `{key}` was added a second time{onLine}.

entries.title: Argument is not valid
entries.explain: A method checked one of its arguments and rejected it: it is the right type, but its value breaks a rule the method states, such as an empty name, an unknown enum value or a malformed path.
causes: An empty or whitespace string where text is required.
A value that is not one of the allowed options (`Enum.Parse` with an unknown name).
Two arguments that do not fit together, such as an end date before a start date.
fix: Read the message and the `(Parameter '...')` part: they name the rule and the argument.
Validate input before passing it on, or use the `Try...` version of the method if one exists.
entries.before: var color = Enum.Parse<ConsoleColor>("Purple");   // not a ConsoleColor
entries.after:
if (Enum.TryParse<ConsoleColor>("Purple", out var color))
    Console.ForegroundColor = color;
entries.specific: The message says: {detail}.

entries.title: Attempted to divide by zero
entries.explain: Integer and `decimal` division (`/` and `%`) by zero has no answer, so .NET throws. Note that `double` and `float` do not throw: dividing them by zero gives `Infinity` or `NaN` instead.
causes: Computing an average with `sum / count` when `count` is `0` (an empty list).
A divisor read from input or calculated, which happened to be `0`.
`x % 0` when checking divisibility.
fix: Check the divisor first: `var avg = count == 0 ? 0 : sum / count;`.
For averages of lists, guard with `if (items.Count > 0)`.
entries.before:
int sum = 0, count = 0;
int average = sum / count;   // throws
entries.after:
int sum = 0, count = 0;
int average = count == 0 ? 0 : sum / count;

hunt.note: Line {line} divides with `{match}`; check whether the right-hand side can be 0.

entries.specific: A division{onLine} had 0 on the right.

entries.title: Arithmetic operation resulted in an overflow
entries.explain: A number got too big or too small for its type: an `int` holds roughly plus or minus 2.1 billion. Plain integer arithmetic silently wraps around by default, so this exception comes from a `checked` block, a conversion (`Convert.ToInt32`, `int.Parse`, casting a large `decimal`) or `decimal` arithmetic.
causes: Parsing text whose number does not fit: `int.Parse("3000000000")`.
Converting a large `long`, `double` or `decimal` to `int` with `Convert.ToInt32` or in a `checked` context.
A running total or product (such as a factorial) that grows past the type's maximum.
fix: Use a larger type: `long`, `decimal`, or `System.Numerics.BigInteger` for very large values.
Use `TryParse` for input so out-of-range text is handled, not thrown.
entries.before: int big = int.Parse("3000000000");   // too large for int
entries.after: long big = long.Parse("3000000000");
entries.specific: A value did not fit in its numeric type{onLine}.

entries.capture: cast object of type '(?<from>[^']+)' to type '(?<to>[^']+)'
entries.title: Specified cast is not valid
entries.explain: A cast such as `(int)obj` only works when the object really is of that type at run time. A cast does not convert one kind of value into another: an `object` holding the string `"5"` cannot be cast to `int`.
causes: Casting a boxed value to a different type than it was stored as (a boxed `int` cast to `long` also fails).
Casting text to a number instead of parsing it.
Casting a base class to a derived class it is not.
fix: Parse or convert values: `int.Parse(text)`, `Convert.ToInt32(value)`.
Test the type with pattern matching: `if (obj is int n) ...`.
Use `as` for reference types and check for `null`.
entries.before:
object value = "5";
int n = (int)value;   // a string is not an int
entries.after:
object value = "5";
int n = int.Parse((string)value);
entries.specific: A `{from}` was cast to `{to}`{onLine}, but it is not one.

entries.title: Stack overflow
entries.explain: Every method call uses a little memory on the call stack until it returns. A method kept calling itself (directly or through others) without stopping, the stack ran out, and .NET ended the process; this one cannot be caught.
causes: A recursive method with no base case, or a base case that is never reached.
A property that returns or sets itself: `public int Age { get => Age; }` instead of using a backing field.
Two methods or constructors that call each other forever.
fix: Make sure recursion has a base case that every call moves toward (`if (n <= 1) return 1;`).
In properties, read and write a field (`_age`), or use an auto-property `{ get; set; }`.
For very deep work, rewrite the recursion as a loop.
entries.before: int Factorial(int n) => n * Factorial(n - 1);   // never stops
entries.after: int Factorial(int n) => n <= 1 ? 1 : n * Factorial(n - 1);
entries.specific: The program ran out of stack, which almost always means endless recursion.

entries.title: The method or operation is not implemented
entries.explain: Code reached a `throw new NotImplementedException();`. That line is a placeholder, often generated by the editor, that marks a method body nobody has written yet.
causes: A starter method or interface implementation that still has its placeholder body.
An IDE quick fix ("Implement interface") that filled methods with `throw new NotImplementedException()`.
fix: Replace the `throw` with the real logic of the method.
If the method is genuinely not meant to be supported, throw `NotSupportedException` with a clear message instead.

hunt.note: Line {line} is a placeholder that still needs the real code.

entries.specific: A placeholder method body was reached{onLine}.

entries.title: Could not find file
entries.explain: The program tried to open a file that does not exist at the path it used. A relative path such as `data.txt` is looked up from the current working directory, which is often not the folder your source file is in.
causes: A typo in the file name or extension (`data.txt` vs `data.csv`, or hidden `.txt.txt`).
A relative path resolved against a different working directory than you expected.
The file is not copied next to the program when it builds or runs.
fix: Print `Path.GetFullPath("data.txt")` to see where the program is really looking.
Check first with `File.Exists(path)` and handle the missing case.
Build paths from a known folder: `Path.Combine(AppContext.BaseDirectory, "data.txt")`.
entries.before: var text = File.ReadAllText("data.txt");   // not in the working directory
entries.after:
var path = Path.Combine(AppContext.BaseDirectory, "data.txt");
var text = File.Exists(path) ? File.ReadAllText(path) : "";
entries.specific: No file exists at `{path}`.

entries.title: Could not find a part of the path
entries.explain: One of the folders in the path does not exist. Writing a file creates the file, but not the folders above it, and reading needs every folder to be there.
causes: Writing to `output/report.txt` before the `output` folder exists.
A typo in a folder name, or a path built with the wrong separator or a missing part.
A relative path resolved from a different working directory.
fix: Create the folder first: `Directory.CreateDirectory("output");` (it does nothing if it already exists).
Build paths with `Path.Combine` rather than gluing strings.
entries.before: File.WriteAllText("output/report.txt", "done");   // no output folder
entries.after:
Directory.CreateDirectory("output");
File.WriteAllText(Path.Combine("output", "report.txt"), "done");
entries.specific: A folder in `{path}` does not exist.

entries.capture: Access to the path '(?<path>[^']+)' is denied
entries.title: Access to the path is denied
entries.explain: The operating system refused the file operation. Either the account running the program lacks permission, or the path is something that cannot be opened that way, such as a folder passed to a method that expects a file.
causes: Passing a folder path to `File.ReadAllText` or `File.WriteAllText`.
Writing into a protected location (`C:\Program Files`, system folders) or a read-only file.
Another program has the file locked in a way that blocks you.
fix: Check the path points to a file, not a folder.
Write to a folder you own, such as the temp folder (`Path.GetTempPath()`) or the user's documents.
Clear the read-only attribute or close the program holding the file.
entries.before: File.WriteAllText("reports", "total: 4");   // reports is a folder
entries.after: File.WriteAllText(Path.Combine("reports", "total.txt"), "total: 4");
entries.specific: The program is not allowed to use `{path}` that way.

entries.title: An error occurred while saving the entity changes
entries.explain: EF Core sent your changes to the database during `SaveChanges`, and the database rejected them. The real reason is in the inner exception (with SQLite, a `SqliteException` such as `UNIQUE constraint failed` or `FOREIGN KEY constraint failed`).
causes: `UNIQUE constraint failed`: inserting a row whose key or unique column value already exists.
`FOREIGN KEY constraint failed`: a row points at a parent that does not exist (for example `CustomerId = 99`), or deleting a parent that still has children.
`NOT NULL constraint failed`: a required column was left `null`.
The table or column does not exist because the database was not migrated or created (`no such table`).
fix: Print `ex.InnerException?.Message` to see the database's own reason.
For duplicates, look the row up first or let the database generate the key.
For foreign keys, save the parent first, or set the navigation property so EF Core inserts both in order.
For a missing table, run `db.Database.EnsureCreated()` or apply migrations.
entries.before:
db.Orders.Add(new Order { CustomerId = 99 });   // no customer 99
db.SaveChanges();
entries.specific: The database rejected the changes saved{onLine}; the inner exception has the exact constraint.

entries.title: Expected to affect 1 row, but affected 0
entries.explain: EF Core updated or deleted a row by its key and the database reported that no row changed. Either the row no longer exists, or a concurrency token (such as a row version) no longer matches, meaning someone else changed it since it was loaded.
causes: Updating or removing an entity whose row was already deleted.
Attaching an object with a key that does not exist in the table (`Update(new Product { Id = 42 })`).
Another user or context changed the row, so its concurrency token differs.
fix: Load the entity from the database first and change that instance.
Catch `DbUpdateConcurrencyException`, reload the entry (`entry.Reload()`), and decide whose change wins.
entries.before:
db.Products.Remove(new Product { Id = 42 });   // no row 42
db.SaveChanges();
entries.after:
var p = db.Products.Find(42);
if (p is not null) { db.Products.Remove(p); db.SaveChanges(); }
entries.specific: A save{onLine} matched no row in the database.

entries.title: Cannot access a disposed object
entries.explain: The object had already been disposed (closed and its resources released), usually by a `using` block or statement ending, and then the code tried to use it again.
causes: Returning a stream, reader or `DbContext` from inside a `using` block and using it after the block ends.
A lazy LINQ query over a disposed context, run after the `using` ends.
Calling `Dispose()` (or `Close()`) and then reading or writing.
fix: Finish all work with the object inside its `using` scope.
Materialize results with `ToList()` before the scope ends.
Let the caller own the object's lifetime instead of disposing it early.
entries.specific: `{name}` was used after it was disposed.

entries.title: A task was canceled
entries.explain: An async operation stopped before finishing because it was canceled. With `HttpClient` this most often means the request took longer than its `Timeout` (100 seconds by default), not that anyone canceled it on purpose.
causes: An `HttpClient` request timed out (the message mentions `HttpClient.Timeout`).
A `CancellationToken` passed to the call was canceled, for example by a `CancellationTokenSource` with a timeout.
`Task.Delay` or another awaited call was given a token that fired.
fix: For timeouts, check the server or URL, or raise `client.Timeout` if the work is genuinely slow.
Catch `OperationCanceledException` (the base type) where cancellation is an expected outcome.
entries.before:
var client = new HttpClient { Timeout = TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(1) };
var html = await client.GetStringAsync(url);   // times out
entries.specific: An awaited operation{onLine} was canceled or timed out.

entries.title: The operation was canceled
entries.explain: Code that accepts a `CancellationToken` noticed the token was canceled and stopped by throwing. This is how cancellation is meant to work in .NET; it becomes a crash only when nothing catches it.
causes: A `CancellationTokenSource` was canceled, or its `CancelAfter` time ran out.
`token.ThrowIfCancellationRequested()` ran after cancellation.
The app was shutting down and canceled pending work.
fix: Catch `OperationCanceledException` around work that may be canceled and treat it as a normal outcome.
If it should not be canceled, check where the token comes from and how long `CancelAfter` allows.
entries.before:
using var cts = new CancellationTokenSource(TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(10));
await Task.Delay(1000, cts.Token);   // canceled
entries.specific: Work{onLine} was canceled through its cancellation token.

entries.message: JSON value could not be converted to (?<type>[\w.`\[\]]+)(?:\. Path: (?<path>\$[^ |]*))?
entries.title: The JSON value could not be converted
entries.explain: `System.Text.Json` found a value whose JSON kind does not match the C# property's type, for example a string `"42"` for an `int` property, or an object where a list was expected.
causes: Numbers sent as strings (`"age": "42"`) for a numeric property.
A JSON object where your type has a list, or the other way round.
`null` for a non-nullable value type such as `int` or `DateTime`.
fix: Make the C# type match the JSON (`string`, `List<T>`, `int?`).
To accept numbers written as strings, set `NumberHandling = JsonNumberHandling.AllowReadingFromString` in `JsonSerializerOptions`.
entries.before:
record Person(string Name, int Age);
var p = JsonSerializer.Deserialize<Person>("{\"Name\":\"Ann\",\"Age\":\"42\"}");
entries.after:
record Person(string Name, int Age);
var p = JsonSerializer.Deserialize<Person>("{\"Name\":\"Ann\",\"Age\":42}");
entries.specific: The value at `{path}` could not be read as `{type}`.

entries.title: Invalid JSON
entries.explain: `System.Text.Json` could not read the text as JSON, or could not fit it into your type. The `Path`, `LineNumber` and `BytePositionInLine` in the message point at where it gave up (both counted from 0).
causes: The text is not JSON at all, such as an HTML error page or an empty string.
JSON syntax mistakes: single quotes, trailing commas, comments, or unquoted property names (all rejected by default).
The JSON shape does not match the C# type.
fix: Print the text you are parsing; check it really is the JSON you expect.
Use double quotes and remove trailing commas, or enable `AllowTrailingCommas` / `ReadCommentHandling` in `JsonSerializerOptions`.
entries.before: var tags = JsonSerializer.Deserialize<string[]>("['a', 'b',]");
entries.after: var tags = JsonSerializer.Deserialize<string[]>("[\"a\", \"b\"]");
entries.specific: Reading stopped at JSON path `{path}`.

entries.message: status code does not indicate success: (?<status>\d{3})(?: \((?<reason>[^)]*)\))?
entries.title: Response status code does not indicate success
entries.explain: The server answered, but with an error status such as 404 (not found) or 500 (server error). `EnsureSuccessStatusCode()`, and helpers like `GetStringAsync` and `GetFromJsonAsync`, turn any status outside 200-299 into this exception.
causes: A wrong URL or route (404).
Missing or invalid credentials (401, 403).
Invalid request data (400) or a failure on the server (500).
fix: Check `response.StatusCode` yourself when an error status is a normal outcome, instead of calling `EnsureSuccessStatusCode()`.
Read the response body: servers usually explain a 400 or 500 there.
entries.before: var json = await client.GetStringAsync("/api/itmes");   // typo: 404
entries.specific: The server replied with status {status}{onLine}.

entries.title: HTTP request failed
entries.explain: `HttpClient` could not complete the request at the network level: it could not resolve the host name, connect, or establish TLS. No HTTP response came back at all.
causes: A typo in the host name, or no network access ("No such host is known").
Nothing is listening on that address or port ("Connection refused"), such as a local server that is not running.
Using `https` against a server that only speaks `http`, or a certificate problem.
fix: Check the full URL, including scheme and port.
Make sure the server is running and reachable from this machine.
Wrap network calls in `try`/`catch (HttpRequestException)` and report the failure.
entries.before: var html = await client.GetStringAsync("http://localhost:5999/");   // nothing listening
entries.after:
try { var html = await client.GetStringAsync("http://localhost:5000/"); }
catch (HttpRequestException ex) { Console.WriteLine($"Request failed: {ex.Message}"); }
entries.specific: The request to `{host}` did not get a response.

entries.title: SQLite: UNIQUE constraint failed
entries.explain: SQLite refused to insert or update a row because another row already has the same value in a column that must be unique, such as a primary key or an email column with a unique index.
causes: Inserting a row with an `Id` that already exists.
Running the same seed or insert code twice.
Duplicate values in data you import.
fix: Let SQLite generate the key: leave out `INTEGER PRIMARY KEY` values.
Use `INSERT OR IGNORE`, or an upsert: `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT(col) DO UPDATE SET ...`.
Check for an existing row before inserting.
entries.before:
cmd.CommandText = "INSERT INTO users (id, name) VALUES (1, 'Ann')";
cmd.ExecuteNonQuery();   // id 1 already exists
entries.after:
cmd.CommandText = "INSERT INTO users (name) VALUES ('Ann')";
cmd.ExecuteNonQuery();
entries.specific: A value in `{target}` is already used by another row.

entries.title: SQLite error
entries.explain: The SQLite database rejected a command sent from C#. The text after `SQLite Error N:` is SQLite's own message, the same one you would see running the SQL directly; the number is SQLite's result code (1 = general SQL error, 19 = constraint failed).
causes: `no such table` / `no such column`: the schema does not match the SQL (typo, or the table was never created).
`near "...": syntax error`: a mistake in the SQL text.
A constraint (`UNIQUE`, `NOT NULL`, `FOREIGN KEY`, `CHECK`) rejected the data.
fix: Copy the SQL and run it on its own to see the error in isolation.
Use parameters (`$name` with `cmd.Parameters.AddWithValue`) rather than building SQL with string concatenation, which avoids quoting mistakes.
Make sure the tables are created before they are queried.
entries.before: cmd.CommandText = $"SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = {name}";   // unquoted text
entries.after:
cmd.CommandText = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = $name";
cmd.Parameters.AddWithValue("$name", name);
entries.specific: SQLite says: {detail}.
